1. The Beginning

Genesis 1:1

1. The Beginning

Genesis 1:1

The story of Jesus fits within the larger story of the Judeo Christian tradition. The purpose of everything since creation has been to point to the life of Jesus. All of creation speaks of the majesty of God. As God created man and woman he intended them to live in peace with him forever. But because of their disobedience mankind was separated from God. But God still loved mankind so throughout the Scriptures God reveals his plan to save the world.

3:43
2. Birth Of Jesus

Luke 1:1

2. Birth Of Jesus

Luke 1:1

Luke makes his introduction as the careful author of this Gospel. The angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a virgin in Nazareth. He announces to her that she has found favor with God and will give birth to Jesus, the Son of God. Through Jesus' birth, prophecies are fulfilled by the arrangement of events. God leaves no detail unnoticed. The same can be said of our own lives.

2:15
3. Childhood Of Jesus

Luke 2:21

3. Childhood Of Jesus

Luke 2:21

One week after the baby is born, He is circumcised and officially named Jesus. While Jesus is a small boy they go to the temple where they meet a man named Simeon. The Holy Spirit had assured Simeon he would not die before seeing the Lord's Messiah. Simeon sees Jesus and declares Him the promised Messiah.

3:47
4. Baptism Of Jesus By John

Luke 3:1

4. Baptism Of Jesus By John

Luke 3:1

John the Baptist calls out in the desert. He preaches by the river Jordan, "Turn away from your sins and be baptized, and God will forgive your sins." He is the one Isaiah predicted would make way for the Lord. The crowds gather. Immediately, he warns them not to only say they have repented. Instead, they're to follow repentance with actions that exhibit a changed heart. Jesus is baptized and receives the Holy Spirit. He kneels at the feet of someone lesser than Himself to be baptized. He demonstrates how we are to be humble.

2:22
5. The Devil Tempts Jesus

Luke 4:1

5. The Devil Tempts Jesus

Luke 4:1

After Jesus has been baptized, He's led by the Spirit into the desert. He spends 40 days there, constantly tempted by the devil. All that time, he eats nothing. The devil tries to tempt Jesus, but Jesus answers using Scripture, resisting him.

3:07
6. Jesus Proclaims Fulfillment Of The Scriptures

Luke 4:14

6. Jesus Proclaims Fulfillment Of The Scriptures

Luke 4:14

When Jesus returns to Nazareth, He goes to the synagogue. He's asked to read the Scriptures and is handed the Book of Isaiah. From it, He reads Isaiah 61:1-2. The prophecy speaks of bringing good news to the poor, proclaiming liberty to the captives, recovery of sight to the blind, freeing the oppressed, and announcing that it's time the Lord will save His people. When He finishes reading, Jesus announces to the people that the prophecy has come true as it was just read.

1:02
7. Parable Of The Pharisee And Tax Collector

Luke 18:9

7. Parable Of The Pharisee And Tax Collector

Luke 18:9

Jesus teaches from a boat off the shore of Lake Gennesaret. He speaks in parables, giving the example of a Pharisee and tax collector going to the temple to pray. The two men approach prayer very differently. The Pharisee in the story stands by himself and lists his respectable attributes. He thanks God that he is not greedy, dishonest, or an adulterer like everyone else. He specifically points out the tax collector and thanks God for not being like him. The Pharisee boldly tells God what he does: He fasts two days a week and gives a tenth of his income. The tax collector stands at a distance from the altar. Head bowed, he beats on his chest. The only thing he prays is, "God, have pity on me, a sinner!"

2:01
8. Miraculous Catch Of Fish

Luke 5:1

8. Miraculous Catch Of Fish

Luke 5:1

Jesus tells the fisherman who owns it to push out farther and let down their nets. The fisherman grumbles that he and the others have already been out all night long. They didn't catch anything. The fisherman agrees to go out and calls to his partners. Jesus sits in the boat with the fisherman. He waits expectantly. Then gathers the nets, slowly bringing something to the surface. He laughs with joy when he sees the nets are full of flopping fish. When they're done, the fisherman sits in a boat full of fish. He looks up to Jesus. The fisherman frowns and says, "Go away from me, Lord. I am a sinful man." Jesus tells him not to be afraid, that from then on, he would be a fisher of men.

9. Jairuss Daughter Brought Back To Life

Luke 8:41

Crowds press in on Jesus as He leaves the synagogue. One voice rises above the others. A man, Jairus, begs Jesus to save his sick, 12-year-old daughter. Another man runs up to Jairus. He tells him not to bother the teacher, that his daughter has died. Jesus turns and tells him not to be afraid. And that if Jairus would believe, his daughter would be well. Jesus and the disciples visit the family. The neighbors wail for the loss of the daughter. She lies lifeless on a cot. Jesus looks at her for a moment. Then He looks to the child’s mother and comforts her. He says the child isn't dead, but that she’s actually just asleep. Jesus sits and looks at the girl for a moment, then tells her to rise.

he Xhosa Psalter of 1850, titled Incwadi yezihlabelelo, came from the mission circle of Lovedale, the Glasgow Missionary Society station founded in 1824 among the amaXhosa of the Tyhume valley. John Bennie, John Ross, and William Govan had opened a press at the station by the 1820s that produced the earliest Xhosa Scripture portions, beginning with the Bennie-Ross Gospel of Luke in 1833.

Bennie, the Scottish teacher who had reached the Cape in 1821, did the greater part of the linguistic analysis of Xhosa and devised the orthography that the Lovedale press and the BFBS adopted. The Psalter drew on Ntsikana's hymn tradition, the revelation-songs composed by the Xhosa prophet Ntsikana kaGabha (d. 1821) that the Glasgow missionaries had preserved and transcribed. Several of the 1850 renderings echo Ntsikana's cadences where the Hebrew parallelism invites them.

The Xhosa full New Testament had been issued in 1846; the complete Bible followed in 1859, making Xhosa one of the earliest southern African languages to receive a full Bible. The 1850 Psalter was distributed through Lovedale, the Tyhume and Kat River circuits, and the Wesleyan stations among the Thembu. The Seventh Frontier War of 1846-1847 had destroyed the first Lovedale buildings; rebuilding under Govan brought the press back to work in 1849.

Sources
Shepherd, Robert H. W. Lovedale, South Africa: The Story of a Century, 1841-1941. Lovedale: Lovedale Press, 1941.
Darlow, T. H., and H. F. Moule. Historical Catalogue of the Printed Editions of Holy Scripture. Vol. 2, Pt. 3. London: BFBS, 1911, entries under Xhosa (Kaffir).
Hodgson, Janet. 'Ntsikana's Great Hymn.' Journal of Religion in Africa 13 (1982).

he volume titled Incwadi yemitandazo, neyemimiselo yokwenziwa kwe-sakramente is not a complete Xhosa Bible but the Xhosa Book of Common Prayer, produced in 1865 for Anglican congregations in the Cape Colony. The full title translates as "The Book of Prayers, and of the Order for the Administration of the Sacraments." The work includes scriptural lectionary passages, canticles from the Psalms, and the Xhosa text of the daily offices.

Xhosa Scripture translation by this date had a substantial history. Wesleyan missionaries at Wesleyville and Mount Coke had printed a Xhosa Gospel of Luke in 1833, the Glasgow Missionary Society had produced further portions through the 1840s, and a full New Testament had appeared in 1846. A complete Bible would be issued through the BFBS in 1859 and revised in the 1880s (Peires 1982).

The 1865 prayer book fits within this translation wave. Anglican missions in the Diocese of Grahamstown, established in 1853 under Bishop John Armstrong, sought a Xhosa liturgy that could carry its congregations through daily and eucharistic worship with scriptural readings in their own language. The translation drew on the vocabulary Ntsikana and early Xhosa Christian poets had shaped for prayer and hymnody from the 1810s onward (Hodgson 1980). Copies circulated in mission schools across the eastern Cape frontier.

Sources
Peires, J. B. The House of Phalo: A History of the Xhosa People in the Days of Their Independence. Berkeley: UC Press, 1982.
Hodgson, Janet. 'Ntsikana's Great Hymn: A Xhosa Expression of Christianity.' Communications, University of Cape Town Centre for African Studies, 1980.

he 1886 Xhosa Bible, bearing the title Incwadi Yezibalo Ezingcwele, e Zetestamente Endala ne Zetestamente Entsha (The Book of Holy Writings, of the Old Testament and the New Testament), was issued by the British and Foreign Bible Society. It represents a revision of the complete Xhosa Scriptures first published by the BFBS in 1859, the product of translation work carried out by Scottish Presbyterian and Wesleyan Methodist missionaries on the eastern Cape frontier.

The textual foundation reaches back to John Bennie and John Ross of the Glasgow Missionary Society, who reduced Xhosa to writing at Tyhume in 1823 and printed a Xhosa reading sheet in 1824. Wesleyan missionaries at Wesleyville produced the Gospel of Luke in 1833, and the first complete New Testament followed in 1846. The 1859 full Bible drew these portions together with Old Testament work carried out at the Lovedale Mission, under William Govan and his successors.

The 1886 revision reflects decades of use by Xhosa Christians, catechists, and the ordained Presbyterian and Methodist clergy who had emerged from Lovedale and the Wesleyan training institutions at Healdtown. Tiyo Soga (1829-1871), the first Xhosa ordained to the Presbyterian ministry, had translated Pilgrim's Progress into Xhosa in 1866 and shaped literary Xhosa vocabulary for biblical discourse; his influence carried into the orthographic and lexical choices of subsequent BFBS editions.

BFBS distribution placed the 1886 volume in mission schools across the Cape Colony, the Transkei, and among Xhosa-speaking migrant communities on the Witwatersrand gold fields after 1886. Darlow and Moule catalogue the edition among the complete Xhosa Bibles issued between 1859 and the major 1908 revision.

Sources
Darlow, T. H., and H. F. Moule. Historical Catalogue of the Printed Editions of Holy Scripture in the Library of the British and Foreign Bible Society, Vol. 2, Pt. 3. London: BFBS, 1911.
Peires, J. B. The House of Phalo: A History of the Xhosa People in the Days of Their Independence. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1982.
Hewson, Leslie A. An Introduction to South African Methodists. Cape Town: Standard Press, 1950.

he 1906 Xhosa Bible, Incwadi Yezibalo Ezingcwele ("The Book of Holy Writings"), is a revised edition of the complete Xhosa Scriptures produced through the joint labor of Wesleyan Methodist, Free Church of Scotland, and Anglican missionaries in the eastern Cape. The Xhosa translation tradition reaches back to John Bennie and the Glasgow Missionary Society's Tyhume station in the 1820s, through William Binnington Boyce's Wesleyan grammar of 1834, to John Whittle Appleyard's complete Xhosa Bible of 1859 printed at the King William's Town Wesleyan press. The Lovedale Institution, founded in 1841 by the Glasgow Missionary Society, became the principal center of Xhosa literary production, with its press issuing Xhosa books and the newspaper Isigidimi samaXosa.

The 1906 Bible printed by the British and Foreign Bible Society in London represents the fruit of the long revision effort that followed Appleyard's original, aiming to correct idiom, align orthography with the maturing literary standard, and restore readings from the Hebrew and Greek. Xhosa-language scholars connected with Lovedale, including successors of Tiyo Soga (1829–1871), the first ordained Xhosa minister and translator of Pilgrim's Progress, contributed to the revision.

The revised Xhosa Bible served the Xhosa congregations of the Ciskei and Transkei and circulated through Lovedale's network of schools and mission stations.
